A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RSHTR research despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, theoretical appendices, experimental details, figures and tables support comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figure 1 report original optimization experiments on Rosenbrock problems, regression, matrix factorization and neural-network classification.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix G report original benchmark experiments, sensitivity studies, classification accuracies and comparisons with additional optimizers.

M1.justification: The Gaussian-subspace eigenvalue procedure remains. However, v2 Algorithm 1 terminates before the final update; v1's update-before-termination ordering survives as Algorithm 5, as Appendix D.4 explains. New Algorithm 6 rejects proposed steps that do not decrease the objective.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Rosenbrock, regression, matrix-factorization and neural-network tasks on the same datasets. Internet Advertisements and masked MovieLens experiments move to Appendix G. Rank and subspace-size sweeps change configurations within retained coverage.

E2.justification: V1 compares against HSODM, RSRN, GD and RSGD. V2 retains these comparisons and adds Adam and AdaGrad for MNIST and CIFAR-10 in Appendix G, Figure 6, substantially extending comparison to practical adaptive optimizers.

E3.justification: V2 reports normalized matrix-factorization objectives and drops gradient norms from the reported evaluation metrics. DNN budgets increase from 600 seconds to 4,000 for MNIST and 16,000 for CIFAR-10, with an additional 1,000 test examples per dataset. The new heuristic comparison uses s=10 instead of the usual 100. These changes prevent treating revised curves as identical-setting comparisons.

E4.justification: V1 illustrates Rosenbrock convergence at r=50 and s=100. V2 adds a rank sweep with r=25,50,100,150 at s=100, testing behavior beyond the rank assumption, and an MF sensitivity study with s=50,100,200. Figure 6 additionally examines optimizer stability across hyperparameter choices.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 1 reports means and standard deviations over eight runs; v2 Figures 4 and 5 report five runs with the same uncertainty convention. Neither version supplies seed identities or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds accuracy, sensitivity and heuristic-comparison results while removing the gradient-norm traces. Table 2 reports RSHTR test accuracies of 0.680 on MNIST and 0.211 on CIFAR-10, versus RSRN's 0.376 and 0.150. New findings include markedly slower convergence when r>s and Adam outperforming RSHTR in speed. These are additional findings, not demonstrated same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: V2 revises the stopping-point gradient/Hessian analysis and adds the condition s=O(n epsilon^(1/tau)) to the global convergence theorems. It changes quadratic-convergence probability bounds and develops dimension-dependent iteration and total computational costs. Appendix C.2 adds line-search proofs, Appendix D.4 analyzes the low-effective-dimensional variant, and Appendix E adds convergence analysis for the rejection variant.

C1.justification: V2 adds total computational and space-complexity superiority over full-space HSODM to its principal contributions. Its contribution list qualifies local quadratic convergence using strong convexity within a low-effective-dimensional subspace, whereas v1's introductory claim referred broadly to Hessian rank deficiency. The headline iteration-rate and stationary-point claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 discusses dimension-dependent accuracy and iteration penalties, interprets the rank/subspace sensitivity tests, and qualifies practical performance through Adam's speed advantage and RSHTR's claimed stability. It attributes moderate test accuracy to limited training data. V1's discussion of unresolved DNN gradient growth and its closing rank-deficiency limitations paragraph disappear, although theoretical restrictions remain elsewhere.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly identifies Lanczos as the implemented eigensolver, documents the added heuristic-comparison hyperparameters and test-sample count, and revises CIFAR-10's stated input shape from 28x28x3 to 32x32x3. Hardware, standard RSHTR parameters, training subsets and the 16-layer network specification are largely retained.

R1.justification: The expanded related-work discussion and Table 1 add positioning against Zhao et al. (2024), Dzahini and Wild (2024), and earlier trust-region work by Erway and Gill. V2 contrasts required subspace dimensions with concurrent work and substantially expands the literature motivating low effective dimensionality.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction and experimental narrative, adds a dedicated related-work subsection, and changes the title. Preliminaries move into the theoretical appendices, classification tasks are presented together, and the appendices are reorganized into preparation, proofs, variants, experimental details and additional experiments.

P2.justification: V1's ten paired loss/gradient panels become eight loss-only panels in Figure 4 and two appendix panels in Figure 5, with changed axes and styling. V2 adds a conceptual illustration, sensitivity figures, heuristic-comparison plots and an accuracy table. Table 1 is expanded and redesigned, and the document adopts conference formatting.

improvement.justification: V2 adds valuable assumption-sensitive experiments, practical baselines and more explicit theoretical analysis. However, it removes gradient-norm evidence and reduces benchmark repetitions. Its new central complexity claim also overreaches: Section 2.3 compares O(epsilon^(-3/2) s^(5/4) n^(7/4)) with O(epsilon^(-3/2) n^2), whose displayed bounds support an advantage for s=o(n^(1/5)), not merely s=o(n) as asserted. These substantive benefits and weaknesses leave the net quality improvement uncertain.
